essays.stem: Describe three ways salon staff share information with each other during a working day, and explain how to make sure messages are clear.
essays.modelAnswer: First, staff talk face to face, for example at a short morning briefing where the supervisor goes through the day's bookings, special requests and any staff changes. Second, they use written information, such as notes in the appointment book, client record cards that show allergies and past services, and the notice board for rotas and rules. Third, they may use phones, such as a staff group message, to share changes like a late client or a missing product. To make sure messages are clear, staff should keep them short and give the key facts: who, what and when. They should speak calmly and politely, and choose a good moment, not in the middle of a client's service unless it is urgent. Written notes should be neat and dated. The person receiving the message should repeat it back or ask questions to check. Private client information should only be shared with staff who need it.
markingPoints: Names a spoken method, such as a briefing or face-to-face talk
Names a written method, such as the appointment book, record cards or notice board
Names a third method, such as a staff phone message
Clear messages: short, key facts, right moment, polite tone, neat and dated
Checks understanding and keeps private information to those who need it

essays.stem: Explain how to listen well to a co-worker, including what you do with your body and what you say.
essays.modelAnswer: Listening well starts with giving the person your full attention. I stop what I am doing if I can, put my phone away and face her. I keep good eye contact, nod now and then, and keep an open posture, with my arms uncrossed and my body turned towards her. My face should show interest, not boredom or annoyance. I let her finish speaking without interrupting or finishing her sentences, even if I think I know what she will say. While she talks, I think about her words, not about my own reply. When she finishes, I sum up what I heard, for example, 'So you feel the cleaning rota is not fair?', and ask questions to check I understand. I show that I understand her feelings, even if I do not agree. Good listening makes co-workers feel respected and helps solve problems before they grow.
markingPoints: Gives full attention: stops other tasks, puts the phone away, faces the person
Positive body language: eye contact, nodding, open posture, interested face
Lets the person finish without interrupting
Sums up and asks questions to check understanding
Shows understanding of feelings; explains why good listening matters

essays.stem: Explain how a junior stylist can contribute to the salon's goals and plans.
essays.modelAnswer: A junior stylist first needs to know the salon's goals, such as more repeat clients, more retail sales or shorter waiting times, so she should listen at meetings and read notices. She can then help in her daily work. She arrives on time, keeps her station clean and ready, and follows the salon's procedures so that services run smoothly. She gives every client good service and suggests suitable products, which helps with sales and return visits. She takes part in team meetings and shares ideas, for example a better way to organise the towel area, using the proper channels. She keeps her commitments and does her share of shared jobs, such as cleaning and restocking. When she is free, she offers to help others. She asks for feedback and training so her skills improve. By doing all of this, she helps the whole team reach its targets.
markingPoints: Finds out the salon's goals (meetings, notices, supervisor)
Supports goals through daily work: punctual, prepared, follows procedures
Good client service and suitable product advice
Shares ideas through the proper channels and takes part in meetings
Keeps commitments, helps others, and seeks feedback and training

essays.stem: Explain why respecting differences in age, culture, religion and ability matters in a salon team, and give examples of respectful behaviour.
essays.modelAnswer: A salon team, like its clients, is made up of people of different ages, cultures, religions, abilities and backgrounds. Respecting these differences matters because everyone has the right to be treated fairly. People who feel respected work better, stay longer and help each other. Different people also bring different skills and ideas, such as knowledge of natural hair, braiding styles or older clients' needs, which helps the salon serve all its clients well. Treating someone badly because of who they are is discrimination, which is wrong and is against workplace rules. Examples of respectful behaviour are using the name a person prefers, not making jokes about accents, religion, age or disability, and allowing for religious days or food choices when planning the rota or a staff lunch. Other examples are listening to the ideas of younger and older staff equally, and helping a co-worker with a disability if she asks. If someone is treated unfairly, staff should speak up or report it.
markingPoints: Everyone has the right to fair treatment; discrimination is wrong and against the rules
Respected staff work better and the team works better
Differences bring skills and ideas that help serve all clients
Gives at least two examples of respectful behaviour
Speaks up or reports unfair treatment

essays.stem: Describe the behaviours that build trust between co-workers and the behaviours that destroy it.
essays.modelAnswer: Trust grows when people are honest and reliable. A trustworthy co-worker tells the truth, even about her own mistakes, and does what she promised, when she promised it. She arrives on time and does her share of the work, such as cleaning the basins on her day. She keeps private things private, whether about clients or co-workers. She gives credit to others for their good work and offers help when someone is busy. She speaks to people directly and politely if there is a problem, instead of talking behind their backs. Trust is destroyed by the opposite behaviours. These include lying, blaming others, gossiping, sharing secrets, taking credit for someone else's idea, and stealing clients or products. Being late often, leaving work for others, breaking promises and being rude also damage trust. Once trust is lost it is hard to rebuild, so staff should protect it every day.
markingPoints: Honesty, including owning up to mistakes
Reliability: keeps promises, punctual, does a fair share
Keeps confidences, gives credit and helps others
Names behaviours that destroy trust (gossip, lying, blaming, stealing clients, rudeness)
Notes that trust is hard to rebuild once lost

essays.stem: Describe how to give and how to receive feedback in a way that keeps a good working relationship.
essays.modelAnswer: To give feedback, I pick a suitable time and a private place, never in front of clients. I talk about the work or the behaviour, not about the person. I start with something positive, then explain clearly what could be better and why, using a real example, such as, 'The client waited ten minutes because the station was not ready.' I suggest a way forward and ask for the other person's view. I keep my voice calm and friendly. To receive feedback, I listen fully without interrupting or making excuses. I ask questions if I do not understand and thank the person, even if the feedback is hard to hear. Then I think about it honestly and use it to improve. If I disagree, I explain my view calmly later. Handled this way, feedback is a normal part of work that helps everyone improve, not a cause of hurt feelings.
markingPoints: Gives feedback privately at a suitable time
Focuses on the work or behaviour, with a positive start and a specific example
Suggests a way forward, asks for the other view, calm tone
Receives feedback by listening, asking questions and thanking
Reflects, improves and disagrees calmly if needed

essays.stem: A dispute between two stylists over a shared station has gone on for a week. Describe the steps to resolve it.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the two stylists should try to talk it through calmly in private, away from clients, at a time when neither is busy. Each one explains the problem from her side using 'I' statements, such as 'I feel stressed when I find the station untidy at two o'clock,' while the other listens without interrupting. They look for a solution both can accept, such as a check list for leaving the station clean and an agreed hand-over time. If they cannot agree, or the problem keeps happening, they should take it to the supervisor. The supervisor listens to both sides, checks the facts and the salon's rules, and helps them agree a fair solution. If needed, she may change the rota or the station plan. The agreement should be written down and checked after a week or two. If it is still not solved, the salon's grievance procedure is followed. Throughout, both stylists stay polite and do not gossip or involve clients.
markingPoints: Talks privately and calmly at a suitable time
Each side explains while the other listens; uses 'I' statements
Looks for a fair, practical solution both accept
Takes it to the supervisor if not solved, then the grievance procedure
Records the agreement, follows up, and keeps it professional with no gossip

essays.stem: Explain what bullying and harassment at work are, and what a worker should do if she experiences or sees them.
essays.modelAnswer: Bullying is repeated behaviour meant to hurt, frighten or put down a person, such as shouting, insults, mocking, leaving someone out on purpose or giving her all the worst jobs. Harassment is unwanted behaviour that offends or upsets a person, for example because of her sex, race, religion or disability. Sexual harassment includes unwanted touching, sexual comments or requests. These behaviours are never acceptable, whether they come from co-workers, managers or clients. A worker who is bullied or harassed should, if she feels safe, tell the person clearly that the behaviour is unwelcome and must stop. She should write down what happened, when, where and who saw it. She should report it to her supervisor or the owner, or to another manager if the supervisor is involved, and follow the salon's policy or grievance procedure. A worker who sees it should not join in, should support the person and should report it. Outside help, such as the Ministry of Labour, can also advise.
markingPoints: Defines bullying as repeated behaviour that hurts or puts down a person
Defines harassment, including sexual harassment, as unwanted, offensive behaviour
Says it can come from co-workers, managers or clients and is never acceptable
Steps: tell the person to stop if safe, keep a record, report and follow the policy
Bystanders do not join in, support the person and report

essays.stem: Explain how to keep a professional relationship with clients, including privacy and personal boundaries.
essays.modelAnswer: A stylist should be friendly with clients but remember that the relationship is a business one. She greets each client politely, uses the name the client prefers and gives everyone the same good service, not just friends. She keeps conversation suitable for work and avoids arguments about politics, religion or other clients. Anything a client shares, such as health problems or family news, is kept private and not repeated to staff or other clients. Record cards are stored safely and only seen by those who need them. The stylist should not give out her home address, borrow money from clients or lend it, or meet clients privately in a way that mixes business and personal life. If a client makes unwanted advances or rude comments, she should say no politely and firmly and tell the supervisor. Keeping these boundaries protects the client, the stylist and the salon's good name.
markingPoints: Friendly but business-like; equal, polite service for all clients
Suitable conversation, avoiding arguments and gossip
Keeps client information and records private
Keeps personal boundaries (money, address, private meetings)
Deals with unwanted advances by refusing politely and telling the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain how a worker can keep good relationships with co-workers during busy, stressful times, such as the Christmas rush.
essays.modelAnswer: Busy times put pressure on everyone, so small problems can turn into arguments. To keep good relationships, staff should plan ahead together, for example at a meeting before the rush to agree the rota, breaks and who does which cleaning jobs. Each person should keep her commitments and arrive on time, because one late person makes the day harder for all. Communication should stay calm and polite, even when the salon is full, and messages should be short and clear. Staff should help each other when they have a gap, and say thank you when helped. They should not take their stress out on co-workers or clients. If someone feels overloaded, she should tell the supervisor early instead of getting angry. Taking proper breaks, drinking water and eating help everyone stay calm. Any disagreement should be put aside for a quiet moment and then talked through privately, not argued in front of clients.
markingPoints: Plans ahead together (rota, breaks, duties)
Keeps commitments and is punctual
Calm, polite, clear communication under pressure
Helps others, thanks them and asks for help early instead of getting angry
Takes breaks, and leaves disagreements for a private talk later

practical1.title: Team meeting role play: agree a fair rota and team plan for the Christmas rush
practical1.brief: As a group, hold a team meeting for a salon getting ready for the Christmas rush. The assessor gives each member a role card with the worker's needs and skills (for example: a stylist who goes to church on Sunday mornings, a nail technician who studies on two evenings, a senior stylist who wants to lead the colour bookings, a junior who is new, and a receptionist), and a salon card with the opening hours, the busiest days and a team goal (for example, cut client waiting time to 10 minutes or sell a set number of gift packs). Choose a chair, a minute-taker and a timekeeper, and change these roles halfway so that more members lead. In stages: (1) write an agenda; (2) each member explains her needs and ideas while the others listen; (3) agree a two-week rota on chart paper that is fair and covers every busy time, with breaks; (4) agree a cleaning and restocking duty list; (5) agree three actions to reach the team goal, with who does what and by when; (6) write the minutes and an action list, and each member signs. Use the made-up names on the cards only. Photos show the papers and hands, not faces, unless the person agrees and the Centre allows it. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Role cards (one per member) and a salon card from the assessor
Chart paper, markers, a ruler and sticky notes
Blank agenda, minutes and action list sheets
A blank two-week rota grid and duty list
A clock or phone timer, and a phone or camera for photos
photos: Sticky notes of each member's needs and ideas on the chart paper
The draft rota with changes marked
The final two-week rota and duty list
The action list for the team goal
checklist: Explained her needs and ideas clearly and politely
Listened without interrupting and showed she understood others' needs
Respected differences such as religious days and study times
Helped reach fair agreements and accepted a compromise
Carried out a meeting role (chair, minute-taker or timekeeper) properly
Took on at least one action with a clear deadline
Helped make sure the rota covers every busy time and includes breaks
safety: Use only the made-up names and details on the cards; do not share real personal information
Keep the meeting area tidy, with bags and chairs out of the walkways
Speak respectfully; no shouting or personal remarks
Plan proper breaks and fair hours in the rota; do not plan anyone to work long hours without rest

practical2.title: Role play: solve workplace problems and record them
practical2.brief: As a group, act out and solve common workplace problems in a salon. The assessor gives you scenario cards, for example: a shared station left untidy; a stylist taking another stylist's regular client; jokes about a new co-worker's accent; a co-worker who is often late, leaving others to cover; and a client who keeps asking a stylist out. Each member leads one scenario as the worker with the problem. Other members play the co-worker, the supervisor and an observer, and the roles change for each scenario. In each scenario the lead member: (1) chooses a suitable time and place; (2) explains the problem calmly using 'I' statements; (3) listens to the other side; (4) agrees a solution, or takes it to the supervisor if it cannot be solved; and (5) fills in an issue record form (what happened, steps taken, outcome and follow-up). The observer completes a feedback sheet on listening, tone and body language and shares it kindly. At the end, the group makes a poster: 'Our salon's steps for solving problems at work'. Photos show the papers and hands, not faces, unless the person agrees and the Centre allows it. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Scenario cards from the assessor (one per member)
Blank issue record forms and observer feedback sheets
Chart paper and markers for the poster
A copy of a sample salon policy on conduct and complaints
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The scenario cards shared out, with roles for each round
A role play in progress (hands, notes and props only)
The finished poster of steps for solving problems
The group's final notes on what worked well
checklist: Chose a suitable private time and place to raise the problem
Explained the problem calmly and assertively, using 'I' statements
Listened to the other side without interrupting
Used open, calm body language and a polite tone
Agreed a fair solution or correctly took it to the supervisor
Completed the issue record form clearly and accurately
Gave kind and useful feedback as the observer
Helped make the poster and took a full part in each role
safety: No physical contact in the role plays; keep a comfortable distance
Stop the role play at once if anyone becomes upset, and tell the assessor
Use only made-up names; do not act out real people from the Centre
Speak respectfully; no swearing, mocking or rude words, even in role
